content: Do you have any idea what assignment can be given to math students in 2026 as a bachelor thesis, so that a student will be able to solve it but prompting LLMs alone won't do it?

Martin Dvořák said:

Do you have any idea what assignment can be given to math students in 2026 as a bachelor thesis, so that a student will be able to solve it but prompting LLMs alone won't do it?

This may be a real hard question these days like , extremely so. Bachelor level math is extremely well studied and there would just be so much there for the LLM.

Besides even if you did think you found such, you cannot falsify that hypothesis given LLM indeterminism, and you can’t really necessarily tell if they did manage to use AI or not in the end :sob:

Learning how to prompt LLMs to write good Lean code, and, in the process, understanding what makes good Lean code (and maybe even why) in the context of whatever mathematics the student is doing, is probably something that can't be done by prompting LLMs alone, and it could also be a good learning outcome for students these days.

Martin Dvořák said:

Do you have any idea what assignment can be given to math students in 2026 as a bachelor thesis, so that a student will be able to solve it but prompting LLMs alone won't do it?

Any assignment which is followed by an extensive oral where the student explains what they have done in real time without access to an LLM.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Martin Dvořák said:

Do you have any idea what assignment can be given to math students in 2026 as a bachelor thesis, so that a student will be able to solve it but prompting LLMs alone won't do it?

The correct antidote to LLM is indeed invigilated assessment , but I think that’s cheating when asking for an assignment idea :see_no_evil: . It being an assignment is the true difficulty :sob: ( assuming assignment in the classic take home and no invigilation) .

Given the topic of this forum, I assume this question is about bachelors thesis projects involving lean, and since I just completed one, I feel like I can contribute my two cents to this conversation.

In my view, ensuring that "prompting LLMs alone won't do it" is unnecessary. If you don't trust the student to be honest about their AI use or follow guidelines you set about AI use, then you probably shouldn't be taking them on as a thesis student (of course I have no idea how much of a say in the matter you have in this at your institution. I mean this more as a matter of principle than practicality.)

While completing my bachelors thesis project, I did briefly check (with the knowledge and prior permission of my advisor) whether AI (Aristotle) could complete some of the formalization that I had already completed, but I wasn't satisfied with its output and so I decided not to use it for the rest of my project.

Additionally the question of AI use become somewhat irrelevant because my code was merged into Mathlib whose standards are far beyond the reach of any AI that currently exists. So, if AI use is a concern, then I think working towards inclusion in Mathlib would be one way to demonstrate that the student's work is of sufficient quality that an AI did not do it, in much the same way that if a bachelors thesis presented content that the student had already published in a peer-reviewed journal, that would guarantee that there was a sufficient level of intellectual engagement with the mathematics on the part of the student. (Again, I mean this in principle. In reality, mileage may vary.)

On the question of choosing a topic, I think that if a student has completed a special topics course in a somewhat beyond-undergraduate topic, they can probably find a gap in Mathlib, and make some contribution, even a small one. I might have personally just been lucky that I had taken a course on C*-algebras, and that there are still many basic results in that area which were not in Mathlib, and that there were Mathlib reviewers willing to contribute a very significant amount of their time to helping make my code Mathlib-quality, but I'd expect/hope that if a student wants to do a formalization project, they will join this Zulip, ask about where they might be able to contribute, and, as they learn to use Lean, get in touch with the appropriate reviewers who will be able to help make their code Mathlib-quality and perhaps be able to identify gaps in Mathlib where an undergraduate might be able to contribute. (Doing these things is also a way to ensure student engagement that is harder to fake with AI.)

(Also, I plan to make a post here on Zulip fairly soon sharing my thesis (Edit: here is the topic: #general > Bachelors Thesis on Formalizing the GNS Construction in Lean), so you can take a look at what my institution was satisfied with in regards to a formalization project as a math thesis, which may or may not be a helpful data point in this conversation.)

I've supervised several undergrad and masters' (and PhD) theses in lean and most of the output has not made it into mathlib. My impression in this case is that Gregory was lucky enough to find an area of mathlib which needed some development at a mathematically appropriate level and also two reviewers in Monica and Jireh who were happy to look at his stuff. Perhaps another data point here is that I have given "do group cohomology" to all three of an undergraduate, a Masters student and a PhD student, for the perhaps selfish reason that I did not really know how to do cohomology theories in dependent type theory at all (this all started in about 2019) and I learnt a lot from my students' struggles! Over time the projects became more ambitious and eventually the work of the PhD student made it into mathlib but it was informed by the work of the others.

In short, whilst "get it into mathlib" is a fabulous outcome for a thesis, I think the stars might have to be aligned in order for it to happen.

Indeed. GNS is conveniently one of those theorems that's important from a conceptual point of view, but that you don't need to apply terribly often, which is why it sat around unfinished. It also waited for a while for us to have docs#PositiveLinearMap.

Of course, this is not to cast aspersions on Gregory's work, as he did a nice job and I think learned a lot during review. It's only an explanation of why it fits into a bit of a niche category.
